opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few reasons these competitions have become such natural benchmarks for us.

The first is that they're genuinely hard for humans. These are the best high school students in the world, people who've trained for years, and even among them only a small fraction earn gold medals. The problems aren't about recalling facts or applying a known formula. Each one is crafted to require real insight, the kind of thing where you stare at it for an hour and then something clicks. So if a model can do well there, it says something meaningful about its reasoning ability, not just its knowledge.

The second is that the problems are novel. Every year the problem committee writes fresh questions, and they work hard to make sure they don't closely resemble anything that's been published before. That makes it a fairly clean test of whether a system can handle something it hasn't seen, which has always been one of the big open questions about these models.

Third, there's a long-horizon aspect to it. On the IMO you have four and a half hours for three problems. That's a lot of sustained thinking: exploring ideas, hitting dead ends, backtracking, building up a proof step by step. For a long time, language models were really good at quick, short answers but struggled to stay coherent and rigorous over that kind of extended effort. Getting there was a real milestone.

And then on the math side specifically, the answers are proofs, not just numbers. You can't guess your way to a gold medal. Your argument has to be complete and convincing to an expert grader. That's a different bar than a lot of benchmarks where you just check whether the final answer matches.

For informatics, it's similar but in a different flavor. You have to design an algorithm, reason about its efficiency, and then actually implement it correctly under time pressure. It tests planning, precision, and creativity all at once.

So taken together, I think these competitions capture something close to what we mean by creative problem solving. And people in the AI community have pointed to them as aspirational targets for years. That history gives them a special weight. When you hit one of those, it's a signal that the field has moved in a real way.

r001.rationale: The response says strong model performance would demonstrate meaningful reasoning and calls the contests aspirational targets, but it does not clearly frame the challenge as matching the performance of the best human competitors.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think the simplest answer is that these competitions represent, in a very concentrated form, some of the hardest reasoning humans do. If you look at the IMO, you're asked to solve six problems over two days, and these are problems that are designed to be genuinely novel. You can't have seen them before. The point is that you have to combine ideas creatively, you have to come up with an insight that isn't a standard technique, and then you have to write down a rigorous proof that convinces a grader of every step. That last part matters a lot. It's not enough to get a number at the end. You have to produce an argument that holds up under scrutiny, and that's a very different skill from what a lot of math benchmarks were testing before.

With the IOI it's a bit different but it's the same spirit. You get a handful of problems, you have five hours, and you need to design an algorithm that's not just correct but efficient enough to pass within time and memory limits. So you have to reason about the structure of the problem, figure out the right abstraction, and then actually implement it without bugs. There's a lot of pressure, there's a time constraint, and you don't get partial credit for having the right idea in your head.

For me what makes them grand challenges for AI is that for a long time they felt genuinely out of reach. These are the kinds of tasks where you can't brute force your way through, and you can't just pattern-match to the training data, because the problems are written specifically so that doesn't work. So they became a natural test of whether a model can really reason, in the sense of sustaining a long chain of thought, exploring different approaches, backing out when something doesn't work, and eventually arriving at something correct and verifiable.

The other thing I'd say is that they're legible. There's a clear bar. The best high school students in the world compete, the grading is well understood, and so if a model gets a gold medal, that means something concrete to people. It's hard to argue with. That combination of difficulty, novelty, and a clear human reference point is what made them feel like the right targets for us.

r001.rationale: The response describes the olympiads as tests of AI reasoning and points to gold-medal performance against the world’s best high school competitors as a concrete benchmark, conveying whether models can match top human performance.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re compelling challenges because they test whether a model can come up with a new idea, rather than just apply a familiar procedure. At the International Mathematical Olympiad, you have to find a proof. You might understand all the concepts in a problem and still have no idea how to put them together. That gap between knowing the material and finding the key insight is a big part of what makes mathematical reasoning hard.

The International Olympiad in Informatics adds another dimension: you have to turn that insight into an algorithm and then implement it correctly and efficiently. A plausible-looking solution isn’t enough. It actually has to work within the constraints.

Both competitions also give us a concrete way to measure progress on very difficult problems. The tasks are self-contained, the standards are demanding, and human contestants spend years developing the skills needed to solve them. So they’re a useful testing ground for whether AI can sustain a line of reasoning, recognize when an approach fails, and find a better one.

r001.rationale: The response calls IMO and IOI demanding tests of AI reasoning and a way to measure progress, but it does not state or clearly imply the specific challenge of matching the best human competitors’ performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re compelling grand challenges because the problems are easy to state but very hard to solve. You don’t need years of specialized background to understand what’s being asked, but solving them can require a really creative insight and a long chain of precise reasoning.

In the Math Olympiad, you have to produce a proof. It’s not enough to recognize a pattern or arrive at the right numerical answer—you have to explain why something is true. In the Informatics Olympiad, you have to turn an insight into an algorithm and then implement it correctly and efficiently. So you’re testing several things together: creativity, reasoning, and the ability to carry an idea through to a verifiable result.

They also give us a clear way to measure progress. These are competitions designed to challenge exceptionally strong human problem solvers, with new problems and established scoring rules. That makes them useful milestones for asking whether AI can tackle unfamiliar problems that demand more than recalling something it’s seen before.

r001.rationale: The response says the Olympiads challenge exceptionally strong human problem solvers and can measure AI progress, but it does not clearly frame the challenge as matching the best human competitors’ performance.
